summary: Proposes a new Telnet option for X.3 PAD, a way to control packet assembly and disassembly behavior for terminals on X.25-style networks. It asked for discussion and suggestions. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: Some old terminals reach computers through a box that packs their typing into packets. This option lets Telnet control how that box behaves.

questions: what is the telnet x.3 pad option
how does telnet control a pad
how does local editing work in telnet
subtitle: A Telnet option for controlling packet assembly and disassembly on X.25 networks.

tldr.problem: Terminals connected across X.25 packet networks need character-level control that X.3 PAD services provide, such as local buffering, echoing, and line editing. Telnet needed a standard way for servers to request and negotiate these services from client terminals.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1053 proposes a new Telnet option (code 30) allowing host and user telnets to exchange messages that set, query, and report on X.3 parameters controlling terminal behavior like echo, line editing, flow control, and padding.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is now Historic. While it provided a bridge between X.25 PAD and Internet Telnet, the technology it addressed has been superseded. Modern terminal emulation handles these functions through different mechanisms.

today: RFC 1053 is Historic. The specification allowed Telnet to control X.3 PAD services for terminals on X.25 networks, providing interoperability at a time when X.25 was the dominant interface between commercial packet networks and the Internet. Modern terminal emulation, VoIP, and SSH have superseded these technologies, making the RFC an artifact of an earlier era of networking.

sections.title: Terminal Control and X.3 PAD Services
sections.content:
When interactive terminals were connected to host computers across networks, system designers wanted to provide the same terminal services as for directly attached terminals. One common approach was to have the host handle all character processing—each keystroke sent as a separate packet. While this gives the host fine control, it creates significant network and host load, especially over long-distance networks.

The CCITT (now ITU-T) developed X.3 PAD (Packet Assembly and Disassembly) services to handle character processing locally on the user's side of the network. Instead of sending every keystroke, a PAD buffer collects input and sends it in larger packets after certain conditions (like receiving a carriage return or a timeout). The PAD also handles output formatting like padding after carriage returns and line folding.

RFC 1053 proposes a Telnet option to allow Internet Telnet implementations to use X.3 services, providing interoperability between the Internet and X.25 networks where X.3 PAD was standard.
sections.eli5: Old terminals connected to computers through a special box that decided how to send keystrokes: all at once, one by one, or after a delay. This option lets Telnet control that box.

sections.title: Negotiation Protocol and Message Types
sections.content:
The X.3-PAD option uses five message types: SET, RESPONSE-SET, IS, RESPONSE-IS, and SEND. The host telnet (the server side) sends SET messages to request parameter changes or SEND to query the current state. The user telnet (the client side) sends IS messages when it makes local changes and RESPONSE-IS in response to queries.

Once DO and WILL have been exchanged (the standard Telnet option handshake), the host can begin negotiating parameters. The user telnet may ignore unrecognized parameters or values it cannot provide. Both telnets must handle the possibility that the peer does not support all features. The protocol includes a synchronization mechanism: the user counts SEND messages and sends exactly one RESPONSE-IS per SEND, so both sides know which response answers which query.

The design prevents infinite negotiation loops by distinguishing between changes initiated locally (IS messages) and negotiation responses (RESPONSE-IS messages). The host, being the one asking questions, is responsible for preventing loops by limiting the number of RESPONSE-SET messages it sends after receiving an IS.
sections.eli5: The server can ask the terminal what it can do, the terminal tells it, and they agree on settings. They take turns asking and answering so neither one gets confused.

sections.title: Parameter Set and Extension Mechanism
sections.content:
The option defines parameters 0 through 255, split into multiple ranges. Parameter 0 (specific to this Telnet option) controls whether the user telnet notifies the host when local user actions change parameters. Parameters 1 through 22 correspond to CCITT X.3 services, including character echo (parameter 2), forwarding characters (parameter 3), idle timeout (parameter 4), flow control (parameters 5 and 12), line editing (parameter 15 with related parameters 16, 17, 18), and padding (parameters 9 and 14).

Parameters 23 through 127 are reserved for potential extensions to X.3. Parameters 128 through 255 form extension sets, allowing new parameter families to be defined for different use cases—for example, Berkeley UNIX terminal emulation or VMS terminal emulation. Extension set 1 (selected by parameter 128 = 1) includes parameters 129 through 138 for additional functions like word delete, custom flow control characters, and bit-width negotiation.

Implementations are not required to support all parameters; they should simply report which ones they know about and which values they can provide for each.
sections.eli5: There are lots of settings: whether to echo, how fast to send, how to handle backspace, and many more. The system lets you add new settings later without breaking old things.

sections.title: Key X.3 Services and Examples
sections.content:
Important X.3 parameters include Parameter 2 (local echo: whether the user sees their own typing), Parameter 3 (forwarding characters: which keys trigger sending the buffer), and Parameter 4 (idle timeout: send the buffer after N tenths of a second with no input). Parameter 13 controls line ending translation between the Telnet CR-LF convention and X.3 padding styles. Parameter 15 enables local editing, allowing the user telnet to handle backspace and line delete locally rather than sending them to the host.

The RFC includes a detailed example negotiation showing a host disabling echo for password entry (SET parameter 2 to 0), the user telnet confirming, the host polling with SEND, and the user responding with a complete list of its current parameter values via RESPONSE-IS. After the host re-enables echo, both sides exchange messages showing the change, with parameter values reflected in the status response.
sections.eli5: For example, when you type a password, the server tells the terminal: "turn off echo so passwords don't show." The terminal agrees and says what settings it has now.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations and Interoperability
sections.content:
The RFC strongly recommends that user telnets support at least the combination of parameters 2=0 (no local echo), 3=126 (forward on any control character), and 4=1 (forward immediately) so that a dissatisfied host can fall back to doing all character handling itself.

The X.3-PAD option overlaps with several other Telnet options. Where X.3-PAD completely subsumes the function of another option—such as ECHO, NAOCRD (padding after carriage return), or NAOLFD (padding after line feed)—the two telnets should prefer X.3-PAD and refuse the other option if both sides support it. The TRANSMIT-BINARY option can modify the interpretation of parameter 13 by suppressing CR-LF translation, but they can coexist. The more complex RCTE (Remote Controlled Transmission and Echo) option provides overlapping services but is considered unimportant due to its scarcity.

The RFC also suggests implementation approaches for specific features, such as using the TIMING-MARK option to properly synchronize discarding of unwanted output when the user presses an interrupt key.
sections.eli5: There are other Telnet options that do similar things, but this one should win if everyone understands it. And there are tricks for implementing things correctly, like knowing when to stop throwing away the server's output.
